(1 row)

postgres=*# SELECT pg_backend_pid(), bal FROM account WHERE name = 'ali';
 pg_backend_pid | bal 
----------------+-----
           1631 | 100
(1 row)

فرایند ۱۶۳۱، مانده ۱۰۰، و سطحی که سرور پس داد همان است که خواسته شد: repeatable read.

نشست ب هم همان‌ها را می‌زند، و بعد فهرست نشست‌های سرور را با لحظهٔ آغاز تراکنشِ هرکدام می‌گیرد:

postgres=# BEGIN ISOLATION LEVEL REPEATABLE READ;
BEGIN
postgres=*# SHOW transaction_isolation;
 transaction_isolation 
-----------------------
 repeatable read
(1 row)

postgres=*# SELECT pg_backend_pid(), bal FROM account WHERE name = 'ali';
 pg_backend_pid | bal 
----------------+-----
           1638 | 100
(1 row)

postgres=*# SELECT pid, state, xact_start::time(3) AS xact_started
postgres-*#   FROM pg_stat_activity WHERE backend_type = 'client backend' ORDER BY pid;
 pid  |        state        | xact_started 
------+---------------------+--------------
 1631 | idle in transaction | 00:51:47.551
 1638 | active              | 00:51:50.827
(2 rows)

فرایند ۱۶۳۸، همان سطح، همان ۱۰۰. و هر دو سطرِ آن فهرست لحظهٔ آغاز تراکنش دارند: ۱۶۳۱ تراکنشش را در ۰۰:۵۱:۴۷٫۵۵۱ باز کرده و همین حالا بی‌کار داخل آن نشسته؛ ۱۶۳۸ در ۰۰:۵۱:۵۰٫۸۲۷، و همین حالا مشغول همین پرسش است. حدود سه ثانیه فاصله، و هر دو باز.

و حالا نوشتنِ اول. نشست الف مانده را ۹۰ می‌کند و مرزش را می‌بندد:

postgres=*# UPDATE account SET bal = 90 WHERE name = 'ali';
UPDATE 1
postgres=*# COMMIT;
COMMIT

هیچ خطایی. مرز نشست الف بسته شد و نوشتنش تعهد شد.

و نوشتنِ دوم، با زمان‌سنج psql روشن تا مدتش هم روی رونوشت بیفتد:

postgres=*# \timing on
Timing is on.
postgres=*# UPDATE account SET bal = 80 WHERE name = 'ali';
ERROR:  could not serialize access due to concurrent update
Time: 1.089 ms
postgres=!# COMMIT;
ROLLBACK
Time: 0.807 ms

یک خط به‌جای UPDATE 1، در ۱٫۰۸۹ میلی‌ثانیه. عددی به این کوچکی یعنی نشست ب پشت چیزی نایستاد؛ درخواستش خوانده و رد شد. و دو نشانهٔ دیگر در همین بلوک: علامت تعجب در اعلان، و ROLLBACKی که به‌جای COMMIT برمی‌گردد.

و مانده، وقتی دیگر هیچ تراکنشی باز نیست — پرسیده از نشست الف:

postgres=# SELECT name, bal FROM account ORDER BY name;
 name | bal 
------+-----
 ali  |  90
 sara | 270
(2 rows)

علی ۹۰. نوشتنِ ۹۰ ماند و نوشتنِ ۸۰ هیچ‌وقت انجام نشد.

همان پنج بلوک و همان پنج نقش، روی مای‌اس‌کیوال ۸٫۴٫۱۱ با InnoDB.

نشست الف اول شمارهٔ اتصال و سطح جاری خودش را می‌پرسد — پیش از آنکه چیزی تنظیم کند — بعد همان سطح را صریح می‌خواهد، تراکنشی باز می‌کند، دوباره می‌پرسد چه گرفته، و مانده علی را می‌خواند:

+-----------------+-------------------------+
| CONNECTION_ID() | @@transaction_isolation |
+-----------------+-------------------------+
|              19 | REPEATABLE-READ         |
+-----------------+-------------------------+
1 row in set (0.01 sec)

mysql> SET SESSION TRANSACTION ISOLATION LEVEL REPEATABLE READ;

mysql> START TRANSACTION;
Query OK, 0 rows affected (0.00 sec)

mysql> SELECT @@transaction_isolation;

| @@transaction_isolation |
+-------------------------+
| REPEATABLE-READ         |
+-------------------------+
1 row in set (0.00 sec)

mysql> SELECT CONNECTION_ID(), bal FROM account WHERE name = 'ali';
+-----------------+------+
| CONNECTION_ID() | bal  |
+-----------------+------+
|              19 |  100 |
+-----------------+------+
1 row in set (0.00 sec)

اتصال ۱۹، و مانده ۱۰۰. و آن پرسش اول، پیش از هر SETی، جواب REPEATABLE-READ داد: روی این موتور همین سطح پیش‌فرض است.

نشست ب همان کارها را می‌کند و بعد دفتر تراکنش‌های InnoDB را می‌خواهد:

|              20 | REPEATABLE-READ         |

1 row in set (0.00 sec)

mysql> SET SESSION TRANSACTION ISOLATION LEVEL REPEATABLE READ;
Query OK, 0 rows affected (0.00 sec)

mysql> START TRANSACTION;

mysql> SELECT @@transaction_isolation;
+-------------------------+
| @@transaction_isolation |
+-------------------------+
| REPEATABLE-READ         |
+-------------------------+
1 row in set (0.00 sec)

| CONNECTION_ID() | bal  |
+-----------------+------+
|              20 |  100 |
+-----------------+------+
1 row in set (0.00 sec)

| trx_mysql_thread_id | trx_state | trx_started         |

|                  19 | RUNNING   | 2026-08-29 00:53:03 |

+---------------------+-----------+---------------------+
2 rows in set (0.01 sec)

اتصال ۲۰، نه ۱۹، با همان سطح و همان ۱۰۰. و آن دفتر دو سطر دارد، هر دو RUNNING: یکی از ۰۰:۵۳:۰۳ و یکی از ۰۰:۵۳:۰۸.

و همان دو نوشتن به همان ترتیب — اول نشست الف، با همان ۹۰:

mysql> UPDATE account SET bal = 90 WHERE name = 'ali';
Query OK, 1 row affected (0.00 sec)
Rows matched: 1  Changed: 1  Warnings: 0

mysql> COMMIT;
Query OK, 0 rows affected (0.01 sec)

یک سطر جور درآمد، یک سطر عوض شد، صفر هشدار. تا اینجا دو موتور یک‌شکل رفتار کرده‌اند.

و اینجا از هم جدا می‌شوند. نشست ب همان ۸۰ را می‌فرستد:

mysql> UPDATE account SET bal = 80 WHERE name = 'ali';
Query OK, 1 row affected (0.00 sec)
Rows matched: 1  Changed: 1  Warnings: 0

mysql> COMMIT;
Query OK, 0 rows affected (0.00 sec)

همان 1 row affected که نشست الف گرفته بود، و یک تعهد که جواب داد.

و جدول، پرسیده از نشست الف:

mysql> SELECT name, bal FROM account ORDER BY name;
+------+------+
| name | bal  |
+------+------+
| ali  |   80 |
| sara |  270 |
+------+------+
2 rows in set (0.00 sec)

علی ۸۰. مانده‌ای که در بخش بالا ۹۰ بود اینجا ۸۰ است، با همان ترتیب و همان نام سطح.

en.title: Isolation Levels in Practice
en.short: The same experiment, the same level name, two engines: PostgreSQL 18.6 kills the second transaction and the balance stays 90; MySQL 8.4.11 commits both without a word and the balance becomes 80
en.body:
Picture a program that runs on both engines and, on both, writes this one phrase: REPEATABLE READ. Both engines know it, both accept it, and both, asked what level they are on, hand that same name back, each in its own spelling.

And one experiment, the very same one, gives those two opposite results.

And the experiment is stage six's, with one difference.

The lost update entry had two sessions that both read Ali's balance as 100; one wrote 90 and committed, the other wrote 80 and committed, and the 90 vanished. No level had been asked for there.

Here both sessions, on both engines, ask for REPEATABLE READ explicitly and both servers report it back. The table is the same, the numbers are the same, and the order is that order: both read, the first writes and commits, the second writes and commits.

On PostgreSQL 18.6: the second transaction dies.

Session A writes 90 and commits without error. Session B's UPDATE answers in 1.089 ms and its answer is a one-line error: could not serialize access due to concurrent update.

One line, and no more. The serializable entry had a three-line error whose second line gave a reason and whose third suggested retrying; this one has neither. And as there, that number says there was no wait.

After it session B is inside a failed transaction and the COMMIT it sends is answered with ROLLBACK. The balance at the end is 90: the first write stands and the second never happened.

On MySQL 8.4.11 with InnoDB: both commit.

The same order and the same two numbers. Session A's UPDATE gets 1 row affected and its commit answers. Session B's UPDATE gets exactly the same 1 row affected and its commit answers too. No error, no warning, no wait.

And the balance at the end is 80 — the very number stage six got at PostgreSQL's default level, only one rung higher this time, at a level both engines call by the same name.

And one more thing that turns this from a curiosity into a problem: both sessions asked what level they were on before setting anything, and the answer was that same REPEATABLE-READ. On this engine it is the default. So a program that asks for no level at all is right here.

And neither engine has broken the standard.

The isolation level entry showed that the SQL standard defines the first three levels by a list of forbidden anomalies, and that the list holds three names. Neither the lost update nor the write skew is one of those three.

So the REPEATABLE READ row of that table says nothing about what was measured here. An engine that kills the second transaction has not broken that row, and neither has an engine that commits both. Where nothing is required, both behaviours are permitted.

And this is not an exception; it is the shape of the thing.

The repeatable read entry had seen another instance of it and deliberately drew no conclusion: PostgreSQL 18.6 produced no phantom read at that level, in that experiment, although the standard permits one. All that was said there was that it is a sentence about one engine, not about the ladder.

Now the other half has arrived: the same level name, on another engine, produces an anomaly PostgreSQL did not produce in this same experiment. One is stricter than the row it claims and the other stays silent where that row is silent, and both conform.

And putting them side by side yields a conclusion. The standard defines this level by a list of forbidden things. An engine implements whatever its own concurrency control makes natural — the multi-version concurrency control entry opened up one of those mechanisms. The two need not meet, and where the list is silent they do not.

So a level name is not a portable contract. It is a request, and its meaning is set by the engine that receives it.

And the question to ask instead.

"What level am I on?" does not answer by itself; these two runs showed one answer meaning two things on two engines. The full question is in three parts: what does this engine, at this level, do about this anomaly? An answer missing any one of the three is not an answer.

And the good thing about that question is that it has an answer, and the answer is cheap. Both runs in this entry were two sessions and a handful of statements: one table, one row both of them go for, two reads, two writes, two COMMITs sent, and one look at the balance at the end. Write the anomaly your program actually cares about in that shape and run it against your own engine at your own level. The result comes back in minutes, and it comes from no table.

And once it comes, it settles what to do, because these two results set two different tasks. Where the engine raises an error the anomaly was caught and its price is one dead transaction, so a retry loop is part of the work — the point the serializable entry made about its own cancellations. Where the engine stays silent, nothing arrives on its own and the ordering has to be asked for explicitly; the next entry shows that on this very experiment.

And exactly what was seen on each engine.

Measured: one ordering, two engines. On PostgreSQL 18.6, two separate sessions, both at the REPEATABLE READ they requested and were reported back, both reading 100, session A committing without error, a one-line error for session B in 1.089 ms, a ROLLBACK in answer to a COMMIT, and a balance of 90 at the end. On MySQL 8.4.11 with InnoDB, the same ordering and the same two numbers, a level that read REPEATABLE-READ even before anything was set, two 1 row affected, two commits without error, and a balance of 80 at the end.

Not claimed here: what other engines, other versions of these two, and other anomalies do. Neither run says any of that — but both show what asking looks like.
en.example:
One ordering, two engines. The data is the same on both: a table called account with two rows, Ali 100 and Sara 270 — the same table and the same two rows as the lost update entry. The order is explicit — each block ran after the one above it, and the sentence before each block says which session issued it.

And that they are two sessions is read off the blocks themselves, in both halves: every read that returns 100 carries the reading session's number in its answer row, and on each engine one of the blocks asks the server and gets back the instant each of the two transactions began — on PostgreSQL from the server's session list and its xact_start column, on MySQL from InnoDB's transaction register.

Five blocks on PostgreSQL 18.6.

Session A opens a transaction at the level it wants, asks the server what it got, and reads Ali's balance:

postgres=# BEGIN ISOLATION LEVEL REPEATABLE READ;
BEGIN
postgres=*# SHOW transaction_isolation;
 transaction_isolation 
-----------------------
 repeatable read
(1 row)

postgres=*# SELECT pg_backend_pid(), bal FROM account WHERE name = 'ali';
 pg_backend_pid | bal 
----------------+-----
           1631 | 100
(1 row)

Process 1631, a balance of 100, and the level the server handed back is the one that was asked for: repeatable read.

Session B issues those same statements, then fetches the server's session list with each session's transaction-start instant:

postgres=# BEGIN ISOLATION LEVEL REPEATABLE READ;
BEGIN
postgres=*# SHOW transaction_isolation;
 transaction_isolation 
-----------------------
 repeatable read
(1 row)

postgres=*# SELECT pg_backend_pid(), bal FROM account WHERE name = 'ali';
 pg_backend_pid | bal 
----------------+-----
           1638 | 100
(1 row)

postgres=*# SELECT pid, state, xact_start::time(3) AS xact_started
postgres-*#   FROM pg_stat_activity WHERE backend_type = 'client backend' ORDER BY pid;
 pid  |        state        | xact_started 
------+---------------------+--------------
 1631 | idle in transaction | 00:51:47.551
 1638 | active              | 00:51:50.827
(2 rows)

Process 1638, the same level, the same 100. And both of its rows carry a transaction-start instant: 1631 opened its transaction at 00:51:47.551 and is sitting idle inside it at this instant; 1638 opened at 00:51:50.827 and is busy with this very question. About three seconds apart, and both open.

And now the first write. Session A sets the balance to 90 and closes its boundary:

postgres=*# UPDATE account SET bal = 90 WHERE name = 'ali';
UPDATE 1
postgres=*# COMMIT;
COMMIT

No error. Session A's boundary is closed and its write is committed.

And the second write, with psql's timer on so its duration lands on the transcript too:

postgres=*# \timing on
Timing is on.
postgres=*# UPDATE account SET bal = 80 WHERE name = 'ali';
ERROR:  could not serialize access due to concurrent update
Time: 1.089 ms
postgres=!# COMMIT;
ROLLBACK
Time: 0.807 ms

One line instead of UPDATE 1, in 1.089 ms. A number that small means session B queued behind nothing; its request was read and refused. And two further marks in the same block: the exclamation point in the prompt, and a ROLLBACK coming back where a COMMIT was sent.

And the balance, with no transaction open any more — asked from session A:

postgres=# SELECT name, bal FROM account ORDER BY name;
 name | bal 
------+-----
 ali  |  90
 sara | 270
(2 rows)

Ali 90. The write of 90 stands and the write of 80 never happened.

The same five blocks in the same five roles, on MySQL 8.4.11 with InnoDB.

Session A first asks for its connection number and its current level — before setting anything — then asks for that same level explicitly, opens a transaction, asks again what it got, and reads Ali's balance:

mysql> SELECT CONNECTION_ID(), @@transaction_isolation;
+-----------------+-------------------------+
| CONNECTION_ID() | @@transaction_isolation |
+-----------------+-------------------------+
|              19 | REPEATABLE-READ         |
+-----------------+-------------------------+
1 row in set (0.01 sec)

mysql> SET SESSION TRANSACTION ISOLATION LEVEL REPEATABLE READ;
Query OK, 0 rows affected (0.00 sec)

mysql> START TRANSACTION;
Query OK, 0 rows affected (0.00 sec)

mysql> SELECT @@transaction_isolation;
+-------------------------+
| @@transaction_isolation |
+-------------------------+
| REPEATABLE-READ         |
+-------------------------+
1 row in set (0.00 sec)

mysql> SELECT CONNECTION_ID(), bal FROM account WHERE name = 'ali';
+-----------------+------+
| CONNECTION_ID() | bal  |
+-----------------+------+
|              19 |  100 |
+-----------------+------+
1 row in set (0.00 sec)

Connection 19, and a balance of 100. And that first question, before any SET, answered REPEATABLE-READ: on this engine that level is the default.

Session B does the same and then asks for InnoDB's own transaction register:

mysql> SELECT CONNECTION_ID(), @@transaction_isolation;
+-----------------+-------------------------+
| CONNECTION_ID() | @@transaction_isolation |
+-----------------+-------------------------+
|              20 | REPEATABLE-READ         |
+-----------------+-------------------------+
1 row in set (0.00 sec)

mysql> SET SESSION TRANSACTION ISOLATION LEVEL REPEATABLE READ;
Query OK, 0 rows affected (0.00 sec)

mysql> START TRANSACTION;
Query OK, 0 rows affected (0.00 sec)

mysql> SELECT @@transaction_isolation;
+-------------------------+
| @@transaction_isolation |
+-------------------------+
| REPEATABLE-READ         |
+-------------------------+
1 row in set (0.00 sec)

mysql> SELECT CONNECTION_ID(), bal FROM account WHERE name = 'ali';
+-----------------+------+
| CONNECTION_ID() | bal  |
+-----------------+------+
|              20 |  100 |
+-----------------+------+
1 row in set (0.00 sec)

mysql> SELECT trx_mysql_thread_id, trx_state, trx_started
    ->   FROM information_schema.innodb_trx ORDER BY trx_mysql_thread_id;
+---------------------+-----------+---------------------+
| trx_mysql_thread_id | trx_state | trx_started         |
+---------------------+-----------+---------------------+
|                  19 | RUNNING   | 2026-08-29 00:53:03 |
|                  20 | RUNNING   | 2026-08-29 00:53:08 |
+---------------------+-----------+---------------------+
2 rows in set (0.01 sec)

Connection 20, not 19, on the same level and with the same 100. And that register has two rows, both RUNNING: one since 00:53:03 and one since 00:53:08.

And the same two writes in the same order — session A first, with that same 90:

mysql> UPDATE account SET bal = 90 WHERE name = 'ali';
Query OK, 1 row affected (0.00 sec)
Rows matched: 1  Changed: 1  Warnings: 0

mysql> COMMIT;
Query OK, 0 rows affected (0.01 sec)

One row matched, one row changed, zero warnings. So far the two engines have behaved identically.

And here they part. Session B sends that same 80:

mysql> UPDATE account SET bal = 80 WHERE name = 'ali';
Query OK, 1 row affected (0.00 sec)
Rows matched: 1  Changed: 1  Warnings: 0

mysql> COMMIT;
Query OK, 0 rows affected (0.00 sec)

The same 1 row affected session A got, and a commit that answered.

And the table, asked from session A:

mysql> SELECT name, bal FROM account ORDER BY name;
+------+------+
| name | bal  |
+------+------+
| ali  |   80 |
| sara |  270 |
+------+------+
2 rows in set (0.00 sec)

Ali 80. The balance that was 90 in the half above is 80 here, with the same ordering and the same level name.

fa.title: قفل صریح سطر
fa.short: قفل را سرِ خواندن می‌گیرد نه سرِ نوشتن: نشست دوم پیش از حساب کردن می‌ایستد، مقدار تازه را می‌خواند، و هیچ نوشتنی گم نمی‌شود
fa.body:
در اجرای دوم مدخل به‌روزرسانی گم‌شده قفل واقعاً گرفته شد و نشست دوم واقعاً ۶۵۲۱٫۰۱۵ میلی‌ثانیه ایستاد. و باز هم یک نوشتن گم شد.

چون قفل جای درستی نیفتاد. سطر وقتی قفل می‌شود که کسی بخواهد رویش بنویسد، و عددی که نوشته می‌شود پیش از آن حساب شده بود — از خواندنی که هیچ قفلی نگرفت. نشست دوم با عددی کهنه در دست ایستاد و با همان عدد راه افتاد.

پس چیزی که کم بود انتظار نبود؛ این بود که انتظار زودتر بیفتد.

قفل صریح سطر (Explicit Row Lock) همین کار را می‌کند. SELECT … FOR UPDATE یعنی «این سطرها را بخوان و همان قفلی را رویشان بگیر که یک UPDATE می‌گرفت». خواندن دیگر بی‌قفل نیست، و هر نشست دیگری که همان سطر را به همین شکل بخواهد پشتش می‌ایستد.

و این یک استثنا بر چیزی است که مدخل کنترل هم‌روندی چندنسخه‌ای نشان داد. آنجا خواندن هیچ‌وقت معطل نمی‌شد، چون نسخهٔ لازمش همیشه در جدول بود. این خواندن معمولی نیست؛ ادعای نوبت است، و نوبت را نمی‌شود از روی یک نسخهٔ کهنه برداشت.

و همان آزمایش، با همین یک تغییر.

جدول همان است و اعداد همان: علی با مانده ۱۰۰، نشست الف که ده کم می‌کند و نشست ب که بیست. سطحی هم خواسته نمی‌شود — همان BEGIN سادهٔ آنجا، روی همان موتور.

نشست الف سطر را با FOR UPDATE می‌خواند و ۱۰۰ می‌گیرد. نشست ب همان دستور را می‌فرستد و دستور برنمی‌گردد.

نشست الف در همان حال از فهرست فرایندهای سرور می‌پرسد و جواب صریح است: فرایند ۱۶۶۰ آنجاست و ستونی که می‌گوید منتظر کیست فرایند ۱۶۵۳ را نام می‌برد. بعد نشست الف ۹۰ را می‌نویسد و تعهد می‌کند.

و حالا تفاوت. دستور نشست ب پس از ۴۲۴۰٫۴۷۳ میلی‌ثانیه جواب می‌دهد، و جوابش ۹۰ است، نه ۱۰۰. نشست ب بیست را از ۹۰ کم می‌کند و ۷۰ می‌نویسد.

مانده در پایان ۷۰ است. هر دو کم کردن در نتیجه‌اند.

و تفاوت با آن اجرا یک جمله است: آنجا نشست دوم ایستاد و بعد نوشت؛ اینجا ایستاد و بعد خواند.

و شرطی که این را کار می‌اندازد.

قفل باید پیش از خواندنی گرفته شود که عددش را نگه می‌داری. اجرای دوم مدخل به‌روزرسانی گم‌شده دقیقاً همین شرط را نداشت — قفل بود، انتظار هم بود، ولی هر دو پس از خواندن — و نتیجه‌اش همان شد که بی‌هیچ قفلی. کاری که FOR UPDATE می‌کند همین جابه‌جایی است، و همهٔ اثرش از همین می‌آید.

و بهایش همان چیزی است که در فهرست سرور دیده شد: از لحظه‌ای که نشست الف سطر را خواند تا لحظه‌ای که تعهد کرد آن سطر در دست او بود و نشست ب ۴۲۴۰٫۴۷۳ میلی‌ثانیه کاری جز ایستادن نکرد — و هزینهٔ قفلی که در دست می‌ماند در ادامهٔ همین مسیر سنجیده می‌شود.

و آنچه از این آزمایش می‌شود برداشت و آنچه نه.

آنچه اندازه گرفته شد: روی پستگرس ۱۸٫۶، دو نشست جدا و بی هیچ درخواستِ سطح؛ خواندن ۱۰۰ برای نشست الف با FOR UPDATE؛ همان دستور از نشست ب که برنگشت؛ فهرست سرور که فرایند ۱۶۶۰ را منتظر فرایند ۱۶۵۳ نشان داد؛ جواب ۹۰ برای نشست ب پس از ۴۲۴۰٫۴۷۳ میلی‌ثانیه؛ و مانده ۷۰ در پایان.

آنچه اینجا گفته نمی‌شود: اینکه نگه داشتن همین قفل از کجا به بعد خودش مسئله می‌شود. مرحلهٔ بعد همان را می‌گیرد.
fa.example:
دو نشست psql روی پستگرس ۱۸٫۶. جدول account با دو سطر، علی ۱۰۰ و سارا ۲۷۰، و هیچ سطحی درخواست نمی‌شود — همان چیدمان اجرای دوم مدخل به‌روزرسانی گم‌شده. ترتیب صریح است، ولی مثل آنجا پشت‌سرهم نیست: بلوک دوم وقتی زده شد که دستور نشست ب هنوز برنگشته بود.

و اینکه دو نشست‌اند از خودِ بلوک‌ها خوانده می‌شود: هر خواندنی شمارهٔ فرایند خواننده را در همان سطر پاسخ دارد، و فهرستی که وسط کار گرفته می‌شود یکی از آن دو شماره را منتظرِ آن یکی نشان می‌دهد.

نشست الف تراکنشی باز می‌کند و مانده علی را می‌خواند — این بار با FOR UPDATE:

postgres=# BEGIN;
BEGIN
postgres=*# SELECT pg_backend_pid(), bal FROM account WHERE name = 'ali' FOR UPDATE;
 pg_backend_pid | bal 
----------------+-----
           1653 | 100
(1 row)

فرایند ۱۶۵۳، مانده ۱۰۰.

حالا نشست ب تراکنشی باز می‌کند و دقیقاً همان دستور را می‌فرستد. جوابی نمی‌آید؛ نشست ب همان‌جا می‌ماند.

و نشست الف، در همان حال: اول از سرور می‌پرسد چه کسی منتظر چه کسی است، بعد ۹۰ را می‌نویسد و تعهد می‌کند:

postgres=*# SELECT pid, state, pg_blocking_pids(pid) AS blocked_by, left(query, 40) AS query
postgres-*#   FROM pg_stat_activity WHERE backend_type = 'client backend' ORDER BY pid;
 pid  | state  | blocked_by |                  query                   
------+--------+------------+------------------------------------------
 1653 | active | {}         | SELECT pid, state, pg_blocking_pids(pid)
 1660 | active | {1653}     | SELECT pg_backend_pid(), bal FROM accoun
(2 rows)

postgres=*# UPDATE account SET bal = 90 WHERE name = 'ali';
UPDATE 1
postgres=*# COMMIT;
COMMIT

دو فرایند در فهرست‌اند و ستون blocked_by این بار برای یکی‌شان خالی نیست: مقابل ۱۶۶۰ نوشته {1653}. یعنی سرور خودش می‌گوید کدام نشست پشت کدام ایستاده. و متن دستوری که ۱۶۶۰ رویش ایستاده — بریده در چهل حرف — همان SELECT است.

و رونوشت نشست ب، یکجا و بی‌بریدگی، از لحظه‌ای که زمان‌سنج را روشن کرد. بلوک بالا وسط این یکی افتاده است: پس از آنکه SELECT فرستاده شد و پیش از آنکه جواب بدهد.

postgres=# \timing on
Timing is on.
postgres=# BEGIN;
BEGIN
Time: 0.641 ms
postgres=*# SELECT pg_backend_pid(), bal FROM account WHERE name = 'ali' FOR UPDATE;
 pg_backend_pid | bal 
----------------+-----
           1660 |  90
(1 row)

Time: 4240.473 ms (00:04.240)
postgres=*# UPDATE account SET bal = 70 WHERE name = 'ali';
UPDATE 1
Time: 1.977 ms
postgres=*# COMMIT;
COMMIT
Time: 2.655 ms
postgres=# SELECT name, bal FROM account ORDER BY name;
 name | bal 
------+-----
 ali  |  70
 sara | 270
(2 rows)

Time: 0.759 ms

مقدار ۹۰، پس از ۴۲۴۰٫۴۷۳ میلی‌ثانیه ایستادن. یعنی نشست ب نه فقط ایستاد، که پس از ایستادن مقدار تازه را گرفت — همان ۹۰ که نشست الف نوشته بود.

بعد ۷۰ را می‌نویسد و تعهد می‌کند، و جدول در پایان علی ۷۰ دارد. ۱۰۰ منهای ده منهای بیست، و هیچ‌کدام از دو کم کردن گم نشد.

en.title: Explicit Row Lock
en.short: It takes the lock on the read instead of on the write: the second session stands before it calculates, reads the fresh value, and no write is lost
en.body:
In the lost update entry's second run the lock was real and the second session really did stand for 6521.015 ms. And a write was lost all the same.

Because the lock did not land in the right place. A row is locked when somebody wants to write to it, and the number being written had been worked out before that — from a read that took no lock at all. The second session stopped holding a stale number and started again holding the same one.

So what was missing was not the wait; it was that the wait should fall earlier.

An explicit row lock does exactly that. SELECT … FOR UPDATE means "read these rows and take on them the same lock an UPDATE would have taken". The read is no longer unlocked, and any other session asking for that row the same way queues behind it.

And this is an exception to what the multi-version concurrency control entry showed. There a read never waited, because the version it needed was always in the table. This is not an ordinary read; it is a claim on a turn, and a turn cannot be taken off an old version.

And the same experiment, with that one change.

The table is the same and the numbers are the same: Ali with a balance of 100, session A taking ten off and session B taking twenty. No level is asked for either — the same bare BEGIN as there, on the same engine.

Session A reads the row with FOR UPDATE and gets 100. Session B sends the same statement and the statement does not come back.

Session A, while that is so, asks the server's process list, and the answer is explicit: process 1660 is there and the column saying who it is waiting for names process 1653. Then session A writes 90 and commits.

And now the difference. Session B's statement answers after 4240.473 ms, and its answer is 90, not 100. Session B takes twenty off 90 and writes 70.

The balance at the end is 70. Both subtractions are in the result.

And the difference from that run is one sentence: there the second session stood and then wrote; here it stood and then read.

And the condition that makes this work.

The lock has to be taken before the read whose number you keep. The lost update entry's second run lacked exactly that condition — there was a lock and there was a wait, but both after the read — and its outcome was the one it would have had with no lock at all. What FOR UPDATE does is that move, and all of its effect comes from it.

And its price is the one visible in the server's list: from the moment session A read the row to the moment it committed, that row was in its hands and session B did nothing for 4240.473 ms but stand — and what a lock costs while it is held is measured further along this path.

And what can be taken from this experiment, and what cannot.

Measured: on PostgreSQL 18.6, two separate sessions and no level requested; a read of 100 for session A with FOR UPDATE; the same statement from session B, which did not come back; a server list showing process 1660 waiting for process 1653; an answer of 90 for session B after 4240.473 ms; and a balance of 70 at the end.

Not claimed here: from what point on holding this lock becomes a problem of its own. The next stage takes that up.

Two psql sessions on PostgreSQL 18.6. Table account with two rows, Ali 100 and Sara 270, and no level is asked for — the setup of the lost update entry's second run. The order is explicit, but as there it is not consecutive: the second block was issued while session B's statement had still not come back.

And that they are two sessions is read off the blocks themselves: every read carries the reading session's process number in its answer row, and a list taken midway shows one of those two numbers waiting for the other.

Session A opens a transaction and reads Ali's balance — this time with FOR UPDATE:

postgres=# BEGIN;
BEGIN
postgres=*# SELECT pg_backend_pid(), bal FROM account WHERE name = 'ali' FOR UPDATE;
 pg_backend_pid | bal 
----------------+-----
           1653 | 100
(1 row)

Process 1653, a balance of 100.

Now session B opens a transaction and sends exactly the same statement. No answer comes; session B stays where it is.

And session A, while that is so: first it asks the server who is waiting for whom, then it writes 90 and commits:

postgres=*# SELECT pid, state, pg_blocking_pids(pid) AS blocked_by, left(query, 40) AS query
postgres-*#   FROM pg_stat_activity WHERE backend_type = 'client backend' ORDER BY pid;
 pid  | state  | blocked_by |                  query                   
------+--------+------------+------------------------------------------
 1653 | active | {}         | SELECT pid, state, pg_blocking_pids(pid)
 1660 | active | {1653}     | SELECT pg_backend_pid(), bal FROM accoun
(2 rows)

postgres=*# UPDATE account SET bal = 90 WHERE name = 'ali';
UPDATE 1
postgres=*# COMMIT;
COMMIT

Two processes are in the list, and the blocked_by column is not empty for one of them this time: against 1660 it reads {1653}. The server itself is saying which session is queued behind which. And the text of the statement 1660 is queued on — cut at forty characters — is that SELECT.

And session B's transcript, unbroken, from the moment it turned the timer on. The block above falls inside this one: after the SELECT was sent and before it answered.

postgres=# \timing on
Timing is on.
postgres=# BEGIN;
BEGIN
Time: 0.641 ms
postgres=*# SELECT pg_backend_pid(), bal FROM account WHERE name = 'ali' FOR UPDATE;
 pg_backend_pid | bal 
----------------+-----
           1660 |  90
(1 row)

Time: 4240.473 ms (00:04.240)
postgres=*# UPDATE account SET bal = 70 WHERE name = 'ali';
UPDATE 1
Time: 1.977 ms
postgres=*# COMMIT;
COMMIT
Time: 2.655 ms
postgres=# SELECT name, bal FROM account ORDER BY name;
 name | bal 
------+-----
 ali  |  70
 sara | 270
(2 rows)

Time: 0.759 ms

The value 90, after 4240.473 ms of standing. So session B did not merely stand; after standing it got the fresh value — the very 90 session A had written.

Then it writes 70 and commits, and the table at the end has Ali at 70. 100 minus ten minus twenty, and neither subtraction was lost.
